metaDescription: Five compact cordless drills under $75 compared on chuck size, torque claims, weight and charging, with advice on how small is small enough.
expertTake: Compact at this price means one of two things: a full 20V drill with a short body, or a small 8V to 12V drill built for light screws. The BLACK+DECKER brushless 1/2-inch drill is the best overall because it pairs a compact body with 486 in-lbs of claimed torque and a metal chuck. The Craftsman CMCD702D1 is the plain-vanilla alternative, and the DEKOPRO 8V is the pick for kids' projects and small repairs. If you want to drill holes bigger than 1/2 inch, buy a full-size drill instead.
introParagraphs: A compact drill earns its place when full-size tools do not fit: inside a cabinet, between joists, above your head on a ladder or in hands that tire quickly. Manufacturers use the word loosely, and it can describe a short body, a light battery or simply a smaller size that is less capable.

This guide separates genuinely compact drills from small ones that cannot do much. It explains how chuck size, voltage and battery weight change the feel of the tool, and which trade-offs make sense under a seventy-five dollar cap. The quick picks are above, and the reviews below show where each drill earns its keep.

products.name: BLACK+DECKER 20V MAX POWERCONNECT Brushless 1/2-Inch Drill, 2Ah

specList.label: Claimed runtime
specList.value: Up to 92 holes per charge (maker figure)

products.description:
This B+D is the best compact buy because it does not trade capability for size. A brushless motor wastes less energy as heat, so a short housing can still deliver 486 inch-pounds of claimed torque, the highest in the roundup, and the maker's own claim of 92 holes per charge suggests the pack goes far. The 1/2-inch metal chuck accepts larger shanks than the 3/8-inch plastic-backed chucks on most small drills.

The metal, single-sleeve chuck is the second reason to pick it. A single-sleeve design lets you tighten the bit with one hand, and metal jaws stay concentric longer than the cheap alloys in the DEKOPRO drills. Against the Craftsman CMCD702D1, which uses a brushed motor and a 300 unit-watts-out claim, the B+D's brushless motor gives more run time from the same 2 Ah class of battery.

The cost of compactness is capacity. A 2 Ah pack is light and small, but it will not drive 3-inch structural screws all afternoon, and the POWERCONNECT platform leans toward household tools, not job-site gear. As a first cordless drill it is excellent, and the battery fits the maker's trimmers, vacuums and other home tools.
products.bestFor: Homeowners who want a real drill that is still small enough for tight spaces.
pros: Brushless motor delivers the highest torque claim here
1/2-inch metal chuck takes larger bits securely
Single-sleeve chuck tightens with one hand
Battery fits other POWERCONNECT home tools
cons: 2 Ah pack limits long structural-screw sessions
Platform leans toward light household tools
Costs more than the small no-name drills

products.name: CRAFTSMAN V20 CMCD702D1 1/2-Inch Cordless Drill, 2Ah

specList.label: Claimed runtime
specList.value: Up to 90 holes per charge (maker figure)

products.description:
The CMCD702D1 is the brushed-motor counterpart to the B+D, with the same 2 Ah pack class and a 1/2-inch chuck. Craftsman quotes 300 unit watts out, a measure of power delivered at the chuck that is easier to trust than a peak torque number, because it combines speed and torque into one rating. It claims about 90 holes per charge, two fewer than the B+D, which is within the noise of how those claims are measured.

Because the motor uses brushes, the drill generates more heat and wears faster than a brushless design under heavy use, but for occasional drilling it is fine. The body is compact and light, and the V20 pack fits Craftsman's trimmers, blowers and saws, so it sits on a platform that is easy to expand. Against the DEKOPRO 12V, it is twice the battery and a larger chuck.

Its position in this guide is as the dependable middle: not as strong as the B+D, not as small as the DEKOPRO. Wipe vents with a dry cloth after dusty jobs, and keep the pack away from heat. If the B+D is out of stock this is the one to buy.
products.bestFor: Buyers who want a familiar brand and a 1/2-inch chuck without paying for brushless.
pros: Publishes a power figure in UWO, which is easier to compare
1/2-inch chuck accepts larger bits than the 3/8-inch drills
V20 platform shares packs with other Craftsman tools
Light and short enough for cabinet and shelf work
cons: Brushed motor runs hotter and wears faster than brushless
2 Ah pack is modest for long jobs
Less claimed torque than the B+D

products.name: COMOWARE 20V Cordless Drill Kit with Bits and Storage Case
products.description:
The COMOWARE is compact in the sense of a small, light drill with a 3/8-inch chuck and a 1.5 Ah pack. Its 266 inch-pound claim, equal to 30 N.m, is honest about its scope, which is furniture assembly, hanging pictures and similar light work. Compared with the B+D's 486 in-lbs, it has roughly half the claimed torque.

What it adds is a kit. A molded case, a bit set and an LED mean you can pick it up and start without shopping for accessories. For anyone who wants to leave a drill in the apartment closet and trust it to work, that completeness counts for more than extra torque.

The small pack is the limit. It will drive a bookcase's worth of screws, but a full day of drilling will drain it. Charge it before a project, and do not leave it plugged in for weeks, since high charge and heat age the cells faster. The 3/8-inch chuck holds bits up to that size, which is enough for most small jobs.
products.bestFor: Apartment owners and first-time buyers who want a complete kit in a small drill.
pros: Complete kit with case, bits and LED
Honest torque claim of 266 in-lbs for light work
20V pack supports longer screws than 8V and 12V drills
Small enough for most household jobs
cons: Roughly half the B+D's claimed torque

products.name: DEKOPRO 12V Cordless Drill, 1.65 lb, 800 rpm
products.description:
The DEKOPRO 12V is the lightest drill in this guide at 1.65 pounds, so it suits overhead work and anyone for whom weight is a barrier. A 12V pack uses fewer cells than a 20V pack, which keeps both battery and drill body small. Its 800 rpm maximum no-load speed tells you it is tuned for driving screws and drilling small holes at low speed.

The trade-off against the B+D is large. The 12V drill has less torque, a smaller chuck and a battery that will not sustain long work. It is the right size for assembling a flat-pack shelf, and the wrong size for drilling pilot holes in dense hardwood. Next to the DEKOPRO 8V it is stronger but heavier, and that is the line to choose between.

Store the pack indoors. Cold garages cut small lithium cells' capacity sharply. Use sharp bits, since the motor has little reserve when a dull bit binds, and avoid pushing hard, which is the commonest way to stall a small drill.
products.bestFor: People with limited hand strength who want the lightest workable drill.
pros: Lightest drill here at 1.65 lb
Slim body fits between cabinet frames
Slow top speed gives good control on plastics
LED helps in dark closets and under sinks
cons: Low torque stalls on long screws
800 rpm ceiling slows drilling in wood
Not suited to hardwood or treated lumber

products.name: DEKOPRO 8V Cordless Mini Drill Set with 42 Accessories, USB-C

specList.label: Limits
specList.value: Wood and plastic, not masonry or hard metal

products.description:
The DEKOPRO 8V is a small screwdriver-class drill, the most compact thing in this guide. It charges through a USB-C cable, so any phone charger can refill it, which removes the proprietary charger that tends to disappear from small tool kits. The listing states clearly that it is for wood and plastic and not suited to masonry or hard metal, which is more honest than most.

Its 42-piece accessory set adds bits for common screws, so you can start straight away. The power is low, with the same 800 rpm ceiling as the 12V model but less torque behind it, so it suits assembling small furniture, mounting hooks and tightening eyeglass-scale hardware.

Because it is so light and small, it is also the safest drill to hand to a teenager or a first-time user. It cannot punish a wrist the way a 20V drill can. Do not buy it as your only drill if you plan to drive screws longer than about 2 inches, and expect to recharge it often.
products.bestFor: Light repairs, hobby projects and anyone who wants a small, USB-charged drill.
pros: Charges over USB-C from any common charger
42-piece accessory set included
Smallest and lightest drill in the roundup
Honest about wood and plastic limits
cons: Cannot drive long screws or drill dense wood

buyingCriteria.explanation: Compact should mean a short head-to-tail length, not just a small battery. A drill with a 1/2-inch metal chuck and a brushless motor, like the BLACK+DECKER, can be physically shorter than a brushed drill of the same power because brushless motors are smaller. Check the listed length where given, and read reviews for how it handles in tight spots. Measure the clearance you actually have: a cabinet bay often limits you to about 8 inches of tool length, which rules out some full-size drills.

buyingCriteria.criterion: Chuck size sets what you can drill
buyingCriteria.explanation: The BLACK+DECKER and Craftsman use 1/2-inch chucks, while the COMOWARE and both DEKOPRO drills use 3/8-inch. A 1/2-inch chuck accepts larger shanks, hole saws and bigger spade bits, and it usually has a more robust metal sleeve. If you drill holes larger than 3/4 inch even occasionally, choose a 1/2-inch drill. The 1/2-inch chucks on the BLACK+DECKER and Craftsman are the practical dividing line if you ever want to run a paddle bit or hole saw.

An 8V drill like the DEKOPRO is a screwdriver with a chuck. A 12V drill handles small screws and pilot holes, and a 20V drill handles most household work. Each step up adds weight, so the real decision is how much drill you can comfortably hold. For overhead work, test the weight. If you are buying for someone with limited grip strength, the 1.65 pound DEKOPRO 12V is worth choosing even over a stronger tool.

A smaller battery keeps the drill compact, but a 1.5 Ah pack like the COMOWARE's runs down faster than the 2 Ah packs on the B+D and Craftsman. Manufacturers claim up to 90 or 92 holes per charge, which assumes small holes in softwood. Plan on fewer in real work. Treat the 90 and 92 holes-per-charge claims as best-case, since they refer to small holes in softwood.

The DEKOPRO 8V charges over USB-C, so you can use a phone charger or a power bank. Others need a proprietary charger that is easy to misplace. A tool that is easy to charge is a tool that is ready when you need it, which matters for something that sits in a drawer for months. A tool that charges from a phone charger is easier to keep ready, and the 8V DEKOPRO is the only one in this guide that does.

Brushless motors make less heat and can be packaged smaller, so a brushless compact drill like the BLACK+DECKER keeps working in a tight housing. Brushed motors such as the Craftsman's are simpler and cheaper but wear brushes over years. For a drill you will keep a decade, brushless is worth the premium. Brushless also helps because a compact housing traps heat, and a cooler motor is a longer-lived one.

specDecoder.meaning: UWO measures the mechanical power delivered at the chuck by combining speed and torque. It is more meaningful than a single peak torque figure because it reflects what the drill can actually sustain. A drill with a UWO rating is easier to compare with other drills that publish it, but not with ones that quote only torque.
specDecoder.watchFor: Only the Craftsman publishes UWO here. Do not compare it directly with the B+D's torque in inch-pounds.

specDecoder.meaning: This is rotational force, and the B+D's 486 in-lbs is a claimed maximum. It tells you how big a screw the drill can drive before stalling. Keep in mind that 486 in-lbs is high for a compact tool and would be unusual at the low end of the price range.
specDecoder.watchFor: Torque claims are measured at stall or peak. A drill rated 486 in-lbs will not sustain that while drilling.

specDecoder.meaning: Manufacturers measure how many holes of a stated size a battery can drill. It gives a sense of capacity. Real battery run time depends on the load, and a drill that drives screws all day uses more charge than one that drills small holes.
specDecoder.watchFor: The Craftsman's 90 and B+D's 92 holes use unspecified test conditions. Treat them as a ranking tool, not a promise.

specDecoder.meaning: This is the chuck speed with no resistance. Both DEKOPRO drills list 800 rpm, which suits screws and small bits. A slow top speed can be an advantage for plastics, because high-speed bits melt thin plastic rather than cutting it.
specDecoder.watchFor: A low top speed slows drilling in wood. If you drill many holes, look for a higher range.

specDecoder.meaning: The chuck's maximum shank diameter is 3/8 or 1/2 inch here. A bigger chuck accepts larger bits and generally holds them better. Metal-sleeve chucks tend to stay tight longer than plastic ones.
specDecoder.watchFor: A 1/2-inch chuck on a cheap drill can still be loose. Check bit runout by spinning it freehand.

howWeEvaluated.title: Real compactness
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at weight, body length and battery size for each drill rather than relying on the word compact. The DEKOPRO 12V at 1.65 pounds and the 8V were the smallest, and the B+D was the most capable for its size.

howWeEvaluated.title: Power for the size
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared claimed torque and UWO relative to size. The B+D's 486 in-lbs set the top mark, and the COMOWARE's 266 set the floor among the 20V drills.

howWeEvaluated.title: Chuck quality
howWeEvaluated.description: We favored 1/2-inch metal single-sleeve chucks because they hold bits better. The B+D and Craftsman led on that measure.

howWeEvaluated.title: Charging and battery
howWeEvaluated.description: We weighed pack capacity and charging convenience, including the 8V's USB-C approach and the 2 Ah packs on the larger drills.

howWeEvaluated.title: Fit across the lineup
howWeEvaluated.description: Each pick was placed by owner type, from tiny repairs to a full compact drill.

howToChoose.intro: Pick the smallest drill that still does your work.
howToChoose.note: Hold the drill at arm's length before buying if you can. Weight tires you faster than power helps.
The top tier is worth it if you will use the drill often.

howToChoose.intro: Chuck size is the quiet limit of a compact drill.

cards.label: 3/8-inch chuck
cards.text: The COMOWARE and both DEKOPRO drills use 3/8-inch chucks, which keep weight low and cover most screwdriver and twist bits. They cannot hold large hole saws or big spade bits.

cards.label: 1/2-inch chuck
cards.text: The B+D and Craftsman accept larger shanks and generally hold bits more securely. They are slightly heavier but far more versatile.

howToChoose.note: If you might drill larger holes, choose the 1/2-inch drills. For small screws only, 3/8-inch is enough.

howToChoose.intro: How you recharge affects how often you use the drill.
howToChoose.note: Buy a spare pack if you use the drill more than weekly.

howToChoose.subheading: For Cabinet and Overhead Work Specifically
howToChoose.intro: Tight spaces and raised arms are the point of a compact drill.

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: Low weight, a short head and a work light. Overhead work multiplies the weight of the tool, so every ounce counts.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The DEKOPRO 12V and 8V are lightest, while the B+D offers the best power for its size. The Craftsman is a balanced middle.

howToChoose.intro: The line between compact and underpowered is thin.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: You want a drill you will keep ten years. The BLACK+DECKER brushless is the pick, and stepping up to a premium compact brand adds an even better chuck and battery.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: Your jobs are a few screws a month. The DEKOPRO 12V or 8V is enough.

maintenance.why: Dust causes slipping. Blow out the jaws with compressed air.
Blocked vents overheat the motor. Wipe them clear.
Lithium cells degrade at full charge. Store at half charge.
Vibration loosens it. Tighten firmly with a final turn.
A dull bit makes a small motor stall. Replace rather than push.

faq.q: Is a compact drill powerful enough for everyday jobs?
faq.a: A compact 20V drill with a brushless motor, like the BLACK+DECKER, is. 8V and 12V drills handle light screws and pilot holes only. A short drill is better in cabinets, but a long one often has the bigger battery.

faq.q: Should I get a 1/2-inch or 3/8-inch chuck?
faq.a: Choose 1/2-inch if you may drill holes above 3/4 inch or use bigger bits. 3/8-inch is fine for small screws and bits. The trade-off between chuck size and weight is the first decision to make.

faq.q: Can a compact drill drive deck screws?
faq.a: The 20V models can for short runs, but a compact drill will drain its battery quickly. A full-size drill or impact driver suits decking better. For a household of one drill, choose the BLACK+DECKER or Craftsman.
They are convenient and tidy, but the batteries are small. They suit light work and hobby projects.
Unit watts out is a measure of power delivered at the chuck. Higher is stronger, and it is more consistent than peak torque.

faq.q: Will these drills work on masonry?
faq.a: No. Masonry needs a hammer drill. The DEKOPRO 8V explicitly says it is for wood and plastic.
